questions.what: Listing whom to build for, does the developer find every role that comes to the product with a want of its own, each with an objective for it?
Reading an objective, does the developer see which role it is for and what that role gets from the product?
Weighing a piece of work, does the developer see which one objective it brings closer, or that it brings none closer?
After a change, does the developer see from the key results whether to keep it?
Following a scenario, does the developer see, exchange by exchange, how its role goes from asking the product to having what its objective says?
Changing how the product works inside while its roles see the same, does the developer find the UX still true?
Asked by a colleague what the product is, does the reader answer in one sentence that tells what it does?
Reading the gain, does the reader tell what the product would let them do, and so whether it is for them?
Weighing the product against what they would do without it, does the reader grasp why the product solves their problem where that way does not?
Before installing, does the reader see what the product does not do that they might expect of it?
Before installing, does the reader see where the product is not yet fit for use?
After the walkthrough, does the reader see that the product would give them, on work of their own, the gain the opening promised?
Starting with nothing set up, does the reader install the product by the README's steps alone, and see that it works?
Looking at the figure of how the product works, does the reader see how it keeps each gain and what the opening's message says?
Needing more than the README gives, such as fuller use or help, does the reader find where to go next?
Weighing whether they may use the product, does the reader find the terms for them and their team?
Reading from the top, does the reader find each answer just when they come to need it, so they can stop once they have what they came for?
Starting on any part, does the developer see the one idea by which the product gives its UX, and the piece of it the part carries out?
Following a step of the UX's scenarios, does the developer find the one user story that carries it?
Meeting a case no line of the document names, do two developers of different parts reach the same decision from a principle's why?
Facing a decision the stories need, does the developer find the one component that alone decides it?
Starting on a component, does the developer know what kind of thing it is and what it is made with, choosing nothing themselves?
Making one component that writes a data and another that reads it, do two developers join it to the other data the same way?
Following a user story from its role's first request to its end, does the developer see at each step which component acts, along which arrow, and what data it hands on?
Of any story, component or data, does the developer see which objective of the UX needs it, so that what none needs can go?
Setting the product up from nothing, does the developer put each component where it runs and each data where it is kept, and start the product, asking no one?
Making or changing a component or a data, does the developer find the one place its files belong?
Asked whether anything in the product goes untested, does the developer see for each deployment unit which levels cover it, how heavily, and why a level is missing?
Writing a test at one level, does the developer know what to run real, what doubles stand in for, what to cover and when it passes, deciding none of it?
When the unit and architecture tests pass, does the developer know the product does what this document says, leaving to the ux level only the UX to confirm?
Doubting a choice the document makes, such as a tool or a test's weight, does the developer see what would be lost by the other way?
Following a principle while building a part, does the developer find every figure and list asking the same of that part?
Changing how a component works inside while the UX and the principles stay, does the developer find every line of the document still true?

decisions.what: The opening's message: why Turn solves the problem where the usual way does not, in the reader's words
decisions.decided: Asked for a work in one prompt, an AI fills each gap in your request with a guess. It writes by its own idea of what such a work holds, and judges the work by what it meant. So you find what falls short only as you use the work, and mend it yourself. Turn asks you each decision that is yours, and finds the facts itself, before it makes anything. It makes the work by a best practice for that kind of work, such as one for READMEs, and has a fresh AI, which never saw your answers, read it as its user would. What falls short is made again before the work reaches you.

decisions.what: Who meets Turn at its edge, and in which ways
decisions.decided: The user alone, in three ways, each a user story. S1: start Turn with a request, by typing `/turn:up` or, as an AI that asks for a person, by starting `turn:up` as Calling Turn says; it carries the request and the purpose put. S2: answer the point Turn puts; it carries each fact and decision, the design approved, a decision while the work is made, and the work handed over. S3: start Turn with a run's folder, alone or with a change. From O1's intent, a work put to use having decided only what is theirs, the stories also carry these conveniences, which the UX does not list: in S1, where the request does not say the kind, Turn first asks it, and where Turn has no best practice for the kind, it first makes one, putting its points and design to the user, then the work by it; in S2, where a purpose, a fact or the design is wrong, the user says what it should be, and Turn goes on with each point built on it changed; in S3, a run that stopped before the hand-over, as a point was left unanswered or Claude Code ended, goes on from its folder, with every point settled so far and the work as far as made, not committed, asking nothing again, and a change given with the folder makes the work again with it. A fault of Turn's own can end any of them, and the user gets the fault, to send to Turn's makers. A question the rounds cannot meet is no convenience of its own: it goes back to Pin and reaches the user as a decision of S2. The calling AI is no role and no story of its own, as D1 makes it the user; the ways an AI starts and resumes Turn stay, as Calling Turn gives them.
grounds: Agreed with the user, 2026-11-05: the UX, the README and the architecture each show the main flow to their goal, and the conveniences around it are user stories drawn from the UX and its intent, so a convenience added changes the stories alone.

decisions.what: How Turn gives its UX, as one idea
decisions.decided: Every kind of work goes through one course of subagents, which Lane's routes move. The planner settles the kind and hands Pin the work's goal and the kind's questions. Pin settles the design with the user, one point at a time. The generator makes the work from the design, against the kind's best practice. A fresh evaluator answers each question as the work's user would, never given the design. A question not met goes back through Pin to its decision. Once every question is met, the rounds go on with how the work reads. up carries each point to the user, and each answer back, as given.

decisions.what: Turn's principles
decisions.decided: Turn builds on the principles of the plugin best practice, departing from three as before: up is always a subagent; up decides no move, Lane's routes do; Turn does not learn from each run. It adds nine: One course for every kind; Pin alone settles the design; The evaluator has only what the work's user has; What the work says before how it says it; A shortfall goes back to its decision; Each role starts fresh from the run's folder; Passed on as given; Every user meets the same Turn, no line naming who calls it; Turn changes only the work. Each why names KR1.1 or KR1.2 alone, as KR2.1 is gone with O2.
